codex.worst_flaw: Launch should wait until independent checks establish that offline completion and recorded work-start times can reliably verify that technicians completed the safety checklist before starting work.

claude.worst_flaw: Every technician enters the pilot at once and there is no comparison group, so the design cannot separate the reward's effect from the app fixes, offline support and paid checklist time. holistic.reason: Union co-design, paid checklist time, offline support, safety-hold credit and anti-gaming checks make it approvable, but a 30-minute release reward is modest and quiet, so awareness may be limited, though embedding the checklist in the job card and schedule gives decent persistence.

codex.worst_flaw: The pilot introduces the checklist default during the reward measurement window and has no plain-feedback comparison, so it cannot establish whether paid release time adds value beyond the workflow change.

claude.worst_flaw: The only evaluation is a before/after comparison against a rough 35% baseline. holistic.reason: Union co-design, paid time, no-penalty credit for stops, privacy rules and quality sampling remove the main backfire risks, but a six-week reward of 30 minutes release time is modest and low-salience, and lasting change depends on the app friction fixes holding up once the incentive ends.

claude.worst_flaw: No comparison group or predefined harm/cost decision criteria: success is judged by a before/after coverage figure, so the design cannot separate the credit's effect from the workflow fixes and app maturation that happen alongside it.

codex.worst_flaw: Launch should wait until the programme defines when to pause the incentive and how to independently verify that crews performed genuine pre-job safety checks when audits flag rushed or potentially fabricated submissions.

holistic.reason: Union-friendly, workflow-first design with privacy safeguards and no punitive metrics is approvable, but the 30-minute paid-time credit is a weak, easily missed motivator and the real durability comes from the app becoming the default first screen rather than from the incentive itself.

claude.worst_flaw: The pilot cannot tell how much of any gain came from the reward rather than the workflow fixes, because it compares only before and after: it has no comparison group, no plain-support arm and no predefined decision thresholds.

codex.worst_flaw: The pilot lacks a comparison group receiving the same workflow fixes and private feedback without paid time back, so it cannot isolate the reward’s effect on timely, useful reviews.

holistic.reason: It fixes root causes (ownership, backup, protected time) before rewarding, uses a team-level reward with quality sampling that suits sceptical engineers, but the one-hour prize is modest, the 85% bar in the last two weeks may feel distant, and gains may fade once confirmations stop.

codex.worst_flaw: The pilot lacks a comparison with queue fixes and private feedback alone, so it cannot isolate the meal’s effect on timely, useful reviews.

claude.worst_flaw: The design judges success with a before/after comparison against the 2.6-day baseline plus a follow-up period, with no comparison condition, no predefined success or harm thresholds and no plan for uncertainty, so it cannot separate the effect of the meal reward from the queue fixes or from ordinary variation.

holistic.reason: It fixes the real bottleneck first, uses a transparent, low-pressure, privately-targeted measure with anti-gaming checks, and builds permanent defaults, but the four-week team meal is a weak, low-visibility motivator, and the programme leans on a lot of process (calendar clock, sampling, routing) for 25 sceptical engineers.

claude.worst_flaw: The design has no comparison against plain queue fixes without the reward, and no predefined success, harm or stop thresholds. A before/after change in timeliness therefore cannot show whether the lunch added anything beyond routing, backups and protected review time.

codex.worst_flaw: Without a feedback-only comparison, the pilot cannot tell whether the lunch adds value beyond better routing, protected review time, and timely feedback.

holistic.reason: It fixes the routing and queue problems first, defines the reward tightly enough to resist gaming, and hands over to permanent tool defaults at the end, but a single lunch is a weak draw for sceptical engineers and 'lasting' depends on the queue defaults and how well they stick.

codex.worst_flaw: The reward has a launch-blocking measurement gap because entries deferred for patient care can fall outside the matching window and ambiguous matches can be excluded without limit.

claude.worst_flaw: There is no comparison ward or plain-support arm, and only a single pre-pilot audit serves as the baseline, so the pilot cannot tell what the meal reward adds beyond the workflow fixes. holistic.reason: The design is careful about gaming, fairness and care-first safeguards, but the audit-matching reconciliation adds observer burden and complexity, the reward is modest and team-level, and nothing suggests the logging habit persists once the meal reward ends.

codex.worst_flaw: The pilot lacks a clinical stop rule for a credible drop in observed hand-hygiene compliance, so the reward can continue while a patient-safety concern is investigated.

claude.worst_flaw: The reward pays for a single token kiosk entry per nurse-shift, which has little link to logging completeness or hand-hygiene compliance, and the plan has no comparison or predefined decision rule to show whether the kiosk or the incentive adds value over plain workflow fixes.

holistic.reason: Well-designed pilot that fixes the workflow first, separates logging from clinical outcomes and guards against gaming, but a one-entry-per-shift trigger with a ward-level meal is a weak, diffuse motivator, and retiring the prize leaves only the default kiosk to sustain behaviour.

claude.worst_flaw: There is no comparison arm (no plain kiosk support without the reward) and no predefined decision thresholds, costs or uncertainty handling for the 24-moment-per-ward samples, so the pilot cannot show any incremental value from the incentive. codex.worst_flaw: The reward rule is unfit for launch because an unrelated kiosk entry can satisfy the 30-minute match and count toward the ward’s payout.

holistic.reason: The proposal is unusually careful about safety, privacy, measurement and gaming risks, but a team meal for an 8-week pilot with a shared reward and a sample of about 24 moments per ward gives only a modest push, and logging is a documentation behaviour that will likely fade once rewards stop, even with the workflow improvements.

codex.worst_flaw: Launch is blocked because articles prefilled from ticket resolutions can be published without a required privacy check, so weekly sampling may detect customer data exposure only after it happens.

claude.worst_flaw: It has no comparison group or predefined decision criteria at a feasible sample size, and it never establishes a baseline usefulness rate, so the post-pilot judgement is an uncontrolled before/after claim. holistic.reason: Fixing the workflow first, auditing quality with spot-checks, and guarding CSAT are strong, but the reward is a modest one-hour team prize, so excitement is moderate, and the 12% to 60% jump may fade once the pilot reward ends, even though the embedded workflow should help it stick.

codex.worst_flaw: Without a comparison group receiving the same workflow improvements and feedback, the pilot cannot determine whether the paid-time reward improves coverage.

claude.worst_flaw: The design has no comparison group or plain-support arm, so it cannot tell how much of any rise in coverage comes from the reward rather than the workflow fixes. Its decision rules rest on uncontrolled before/after numbers.

holistic.reason: Fixes workflow friction first, counts finished work with quality sampling, guardrails and a default-based exit plan, but the 30-minute reward is modest and the mid-programme switch to defaults is the real test of whether the behaviour persists.

codex.worst_flaw: Without a comparison group receiving the same workflow improvements and private feedback, the pilot cannot tell whether the paid break adds value.

claude.worst_flaw: The design has no comparison group or predefined decision thresholds and sample size, so it cannot separate the incentive's effect from the workflow fixes or from trend. holistic.reason: Well-designed with friction fixes, quality checks, a clean exit into default workflow and CSAT safeguards, but a 30-minute paid break is a weak reward for a 50% target against a 12% baseline, and the 50% threshold may feel out of reach or be gamed through easy exceptions.
